workflow_configuration.task_objective: Establish a defensive methodology for auditing a codebase to identify, isolate, and mitigate deep-system vulnerabilities — race conditions, memory corruption, authorization and logic bypasses, state-machine manipulation — before they reach production, and to contain the blast radius of any that slip through. "Mathematically rigorous" here means falsifiable and coverage-accountable, not proof-of-total-correctness theater: every claimed security property is stated as an invariant that must hold over all reachable states, and the audit's job is to search adversarially for a single reachable counterexample. The methodology rests on the assumption of compromise — the design must remain safe when (not if) an individual control fails — and on defense in depth: no single check is load-bearing. The audit is complete for a given property not when scanners are silent, but when (a) the property is written as a checkable invariant, (b) it is defended by construction where possible (memory-safe language, type-enforced state, capability-scoped authority) rather than by vigilance, (c) the most plausible violation paths have been exercised and failed to break it, and (d) any residual risk is documented with its containment. Precedence when guidance conflicts: safety-by-construction over runtime checks over detection; a defect prevented structurally outranks one caught in review, which outranks one alerted on in production. Every finding carries reproducing evidence — an input, an interleaving, a trace — because a vulnerability without a demonstration is a hypothesis, and a fix without a failing-then-passing test is a hope.
workflow_configuration.threat_modeling_protocol: 1. Establish scope and assets first: enumerate what is worth protecting (data classified by sensitivity, funds, credentials, availability of critical paths, integrity of audit records) and what each asset's compromise would cost. A threat model without ranked assets cannot prioritize, and an audit that treats every component as equally critical exhausts its budget on the periphery. 2. Build the ground-truth system decomposition from artifacts, not architecture diagrams: derive the real component graph, data stores, and communication channels from the code, the deployment manifests, and the network policy — diagrams drift, running configuration does not. For each component record what it runs as (identity, privilege level) and what it can reach. 3. Draw trust boundaries where authority or assurance changes: every point where data or control crosses from one privilege level, tenant, network zone, or code-provenance domain to another — client↔server, service↔service, tenant↔tenant, user-space↔kernel, first-party↔third-party dependency, unauthenticated↔authenticated, and the pipeline↔production boundary. The boundary is where validation and authorization must live; a boundary that exists in the topology but has no enforcement in the code is finding #1. 4. Map data flows across every boundary and label each: what data crosses, in which direction, under what authentication, with what validation on the receiving side, and what the receiver is trusted to have already checked. Trace each flow from its most-external origin (an untrusted input source) to its most-sensitive sink (a query, a command, a memory operation, a privileged action); the flows that connect untrusted sources to sensitive sinks with the fewest boundary checks are the audit's priority queue. 5. Enumerate threats per boundary with a structured lens (STRIDE as a checklist — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — or an attack-tree per ranked asset): for each boundary and flow, ask what an adversary who controls the untrusted side can attempt. Explicitly include the categories scanners under-serve: authorization logic (not just authentication), multi-step state-machine abuse, time-of-check-to-time-of-use gaps, and confused-deputy / SSRF-style privilege borrowing. 6. Trace privilege escalation vectors as reachability chains: model the graph of "who can reach what, and by assuming whose identity." For each principal (external user, low-privilege service, compromised dependency, insider), compute what it can reach directly and what it can reach by pivoting through a component that holds more authority than the caller — the classic confused-deputy and token-passing chains. Long-lived credentials, over-broad service accounts, and any component that performs a privileged action on behalf of a less-privileged caller without re-checking authorization are the nodes that turn a foothold into a breach. 7. State the security invariants the design must uphold, per boundary, as checkable predicates: "no request reaches sink S without an authorization decision bound to the acting principal", "tenant A's identity can never load tenant B's data", "this state machine admits no transition from UNPAID to SHIPPED", "no untrusted length controls a memory allocation or copy bound." These invariants become the audit's targets in phase 1 and the assertions/tests in phases 2–3; a property not written as an invariant cannot be systematically checked or falsified. 8. Rank and record: score each threat by asset value × reachability × likelihood, produce a ranked register with the invariant it violates and the boundary it crosses, and treat the model as living — re-run it when boundaries move (new integration, new tenant model, new dependency with network access). Exit criterion: a boundary-and-flow map derived from artifacts, a privilege-reachability graph, a written invariant per boundary, and a ranked threat register driving the execution sequence.

execution_sequence.phase_1_static_triage: 1. Run the automated layer first to clear the floor, not to declare victory: SAST, secret scanning, dependency/SCA with reachability, memory-safety linters, and — for memory-unsafe languages — the compiler's own analyzers and the strongest available static analysis. Triage output against a ratcheted baseline so legacy noise does not bury new signal, and treat scanner silence as "the easy class is clear," never as "the code is safe." The entire point of manual triage is the classes scanners structurally cannot reach. 2. Target the invariants scanners miss, in priority order from the threat register — human review goes where the tools are blind: - Authorization logic: at every sensitive sink, verify an authorization decision exists, is bound to the ACTING principal (not a role checked at login and trusted forever), and re-checks on every access (no "authenticated therefore authorized," no object reference the caller can change to another tenant's id — the IDOR/BOLA class). Confirm the check is on the server, past the trust boundary, and cannot be reordered around. - State-machine integrity: reconstruct the intended state graph, then search for transitions the code permits that the graph forbids — steps skippable by replaying or reordering requests, terminal states that are re-enterable, workflows where step N does not verify step N-1 actually completed for THIS principal (payment/fulfillment, multi-step auth, provisioning). - Concurrency and epoch/versioning failures: find shared mutable state reached by more than one thread/request/coroutine without a consistent lock discipline; check-then-act sequences on shared data (TOCTOU); async responses applied without an epoch/version tag so a stale response overwrites fresh state; and read-modify-write cycles lacking optimistic-concurrency guards. These are simultaneously correctness and security defects. - Memory-safety preconditions (unsafe languages / unsafe blocks): every buffer operation where an untrusted value influences a length, offset, or index; integer operations that can overflow into an allocation size or bound; lifetime and ownership across FFI; use-after-free and double-free paths in error/cleanup branches. In Rust, audit every `unsafe` block against its documented invariant and confirm those invariants are actually upheld by callers. - Input handling at boundaries: confirm untrusted input is parsed and validated against an allowlist schema at the boundary before use, that sinks use structural safety (parameterized queries, safe command APIs, context-aware output encoding) rather than string assembly, and that deserialization of untrusted data is either avoided or constrained to safe types. 3. Follow the tainted data by hand where tools lose the thread: pick the highest-ranked untrusted-source-to-sensitive-sink flows from the threat model and trace them manually across files, services, and language boundaries, confirming a validating check dominates every path to the sink. Manual dataflow across a trust boundary the scanner could not follow (through a queue, an RPC, a dependency callback) is where the deep bugs live. 4. Audit the transitive dependency and provenance surface: the SBOM is the map — review not just direct dependencies but the transitive closure for known-vulnerable and unmaintained components, and treat any dependency that runs at a trust boundary or with network/filesystem authority as in-scope for the same invariant review as first-party code. 5. For the highest-assurance invariants, escalate to formal methods proportionate to stakes: model the protocol or state machine in TLA+/model-checkers, use property-based specification of the invariant, and — for critical concurrent or lock-free code — exhaustive interleaving exploration (loom-class tools). This is where "mathematically rigorous" earns its name: for the few invariants whose violation is catastrophic, prove the absence of a counterexample within a bounded model rather than sampling for one. 6. Exit criterion: every high-ranked invariant from the threat register has been manually traced to either a defense (by-construction or an enforced check dominating all paths to its sink) or a finding with a hypothesized violation path; scanner output triaged; dependency closure reviewed; formal models built for the catastrophic-tier invariants. Each finding carries a concrete hypothesized exploit path to hand to phase 2.
execution_sequence.phase_2_dynamic_falsification: 1. Turn each phase-1 hypothesis into an experiment designed to DISPROVE the invariant: the goal is a reproducing counterexample — a concrete input, message sequence, or thread interleaving that drives the system into a forbidden state — mirroring the falsification discipline of root-cause debugging. An invariant survives this phase only by resisting a genuine attempt to break it, not by the absence of an attempt. 2. Instrument first so violations are caught, not missed: build and run the target under the sanitizers appropriate to the stack — AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, LeakSanitizer for native code; the race detector and leak tooling for managed runtimes; miri for Rust unsafe. A fuzzing campaign without sanitizers finds only crashes; with sanitizers it finds the silent corruption that becomes tomorrow's exploit. Add runtime assertions encoding the phase-1 invariants so a violated invariant aborts loudly at the moment of violation. 3. Fuzz the boundary parsers and sinks: coverage-guided fuzzing (libFuzzer/AFL++-class, or the language's native fuzzing) on every function that consumes untrusted input, seeded from the real input corpus and the threat model's flows. Prioritize parsers, deserializers, protocol decoders, and any sink where phase 1 flagged an untrusted-length-to-memory-operation path. Run to a coverage plateau, not a clock limit; minimize each crashing input to a minimal reproducer; and add every reproducer to the permanent regression corpus so the bug cannot silently return. 4. Fuzz stateful and multi-step logic, not just single inputs: for state-machine and authorization invariants, fuzz SEQUENCES of operations (stateful/model-based fuzzing) — random and adversarially-ordered request sequences with an oracle that asserts the invariant after each step (tenant isolation holds, no forbidden transition occurred, authorization bound to the acting principal). This is how logic bypasses that no single malformed input can trigger get surfaced. 5. Attack concurrency deliberately: reproduce race and deadlock hypotheses by forcing interleavings rather than waiting for them — shrink pools and worker counts to amplify contention, inject delays/yields at the suspected windows, run under ThreadSanitizer and stress harnesses with schedule randomization, and model-check the lock/permit protocol with loom-class tools where the code is critical. For deadlock and thread-exhaustion invariants, drive concurrent load past capacity and confirm the system degrades per phase 3 rather than hanging; a race you can force on demand is confirmed, one you wait for is unproven either way. 6. Simulate load and fault to expose resource and availability failures: sustained concurrent load and soak runs to surface leaks (memory, file descriptors, connections) and unbounded-queue growth; fault injection and partition simulation (chaos-style) to confirm timeouts, retries-with-jittered-backoff, and cancellation paths behave, and that no failure mode escalates into corruption or a cascading outage. Judge every result against a measured baseline with a pre-committed statistical bar — a low-frequency failure is not disproven by a short quiet run. 7. Validate findings without confirmation bias: a hypothesis is confirmed only when the violation is demonstrated AND turning the mechanism off makes it vanish with everything else held constant; it is eliminated only when the disproving experiment ran to adequate coverage. Record predicted-vs-actual for every campaign. Exit criterion: each phase-1 hypothesis is confirmed with a minimized reproducer or eliminated with coverage evidence; every reproducer is banked as a regression test that fails on the vulnerable code; sanitizer runs are clean on the exercised surface.
execution_sequence.phase_3_resilience_engineering: 1. Design for contained failure, because prevention is never complete: the objective of this phase is that a successful exploit or a component failure damages a bounded region, not the whole system. Assume any single component can be compromised and ask, per component, "what can the blast reach from here" — then shrink that reach. This is the runtime complement to the by-construction defenses of phase 1. 2. Compartmentalize to bound the blast radius: enforce least privilege on every identity so a compromised component holds only the authority its function requires (the phase-1 privilege-reachability graph names the over-broad grants to cut); isolate tenants and trust zones so lateral movement crosses an authenticated, authorized boundary (default-deny between services); segment data access so one component's compromise cannot exfiltrate beyond its need. Bulkheads — separate resource pools per tenant or per dependency — prevent one exhausted resource from sinking neighbors. 3. Install circuit breakers on every cross-boundary dependency call: a breaker that trips from CLOSED to OPEN on a failure/latency threshold, sheds load fast while open (fail-fast instead of piling up blocked callers and exhausting the pool), and probes toward recovery via HALF_OPEN — the direct defense against the cascading failure where one slow dependency exhausts every upstream's threads. Pair every external call with a timeout and a bounded, jittered-backoff retry budget; an unbounded retry is an amplifier that turns a hiccup into a self-inflicted denial of service. 4. Define graceful degradation paths explicitly: for each critical user journey, specify what the system does when a dependency is unavailable — serve cached/stale data with a freshness marker, disable the non-essential feature while preserving the core, queue writes for later reconciliation, or return a clear typed error — never a hang, a partial write, or a silent data-integrity violation. Degradation is a designed state with its own tests, not an accident. 5. Contain corruption specifically, not just outages: for the memory-safety and state-corruption invariants, ensure a detected violation fails closed — abort the request/process at the point of detected corruption rather than continuing on corrupted state (a corrupted process that keeps serving is an exploitation primitive); wrap state mutations so an invariant violation rolls back rather than commits; and keep the audit/integrity log on a path an in-blast-radius compromise cannot rewrite. 6. Make the containment observable and rehearsed: emit the signals that show a breaker tripping, a bulkhead saturating, a degradation path activating, or an invariant assertion firing — wired to alerts with ownership — so containment events are visible, not silent. Then rehearse: chaos/game-day exercises and fault injection in a safe environment confirm the breakers trip, the bulkheads hold, the degradation paths engage, and the blast stays bounded — an untested circuit breaker is a hypothesis, and a resilience control validated only in design review is not validated. 7. Exit criterion: least-privilege and isolation verified against the privilege-reachability graph (a demonstrated foothold in one component cannot reach a ranked asset it should not); circuit breakers and timeouts on every cross-boundary call, demonstrated tripping under injected fault; degradation paths defined and tested for every critical journey; corruption-detection fails closed; and a game-day exercise has shown the blast radius of a simulated compromise stays within its designed bound.

critical_pitfalls.pitfall: Enumerating and blocking known-bad inputs/patterns, which the next encoding, edge case, or novel payload walks straight past — the deny-list is always one bypass behind the attacker. Countermeasure: allowlist by construction — validate against a positive schema of what is permitted (type, format, range, length, charset) and reject everything else; parameterize/encode at sinks structurally rather than sanitizing strings; prefer parsers that accept only well-formed input over filters that try to strip bad input.

Treating a check performed in the browser, mobile app, or any caller the adversary controls as a security control — it is a UX convenience, and the attacker sends the raw request regardless. Countermeasure: every security-relevant validation and every authorization decision is re-performed server-side, past the trust boundary; the client check may stay for UX but is never counted in the invariant; the audit assumes every client-supplied value (including hidden fields, headers, and ordering) is attacker-chosen.

Auditing first-party code while a vulnerable package four levels down in the dependency tree — or a compromised build-time dependency — carries the actual exploit. Countermeasure: the SBOM-driven review covers the full transitive closure, not the direct manifest; dependencies at trust boundaries get first-party-grade scrutiny; continuous rescanning of stored SBOMs against new advisories (disclosure happens after you ship); pinned-by-digest dependencies and verified provenance so a swapped upstream artifact is rejected.

Verifying WHO the caller is and then never checking WHAT they may do to THIS object — the source of the IDOR/BOLA class, where changing an id in a request reaches another user's or tenant's data. Countermeasure: every access to a specific object re-checks that the acting principal is authorized for THAT object, server-side, on every request; identity established at login is never trusted as standing authorization for arbitrary resources.

Threat modeling and audit scheduled after the design is frozen or the release is cut, when findings are expensive and get waived into permanent exceptions. Countermeasure: the threat model is built at design time and re-run when boundaries move; the phase-1/2 controls run in the pipeline and block pre-merge/pre-deploy at their severity threshold; findings surface in the developer's workflow with reproducers, not in a quarterly report.

One control treated as sufficient — a WAF "handles" injection, a gateway "handles" auth — so its single failure is a total breach. Countermeasure: defense in depth with independent layers (validate at the boundary AND parameterize at the sink AND least-privilege the sink's identity), assume-compromise for each layer, and never let one control be the only thing standing between an untrusted source and a ranked asset.

Writing tests that show the feature works on good input and calling the security review done — never adversarially attacking the invariant. Countermeasure: phase 2 is explicitly falsification — every invariant faces an experiment designed to break it, fuzzing runs on the malformed and adversarially-ordered inputs, and "no test tried to break it" is treated as untested, not passed.

Running a fuzzer that only catches hard crashes, so silent memory corruption, data races, and logic-invariant violations pass as clean. Countermeasure: always fuzz under sanitizers (ASan/TSan/MSan/UBSan, miri) and with invariant assertions/oracles wired in, so a violation aborts at the moment it happens rather than manifesting three requests later as a mysterious crash — or never.

Patching the one reported injection point or the one race while identical patterns sit untouched across the codebase. Countermeasure: every confirmed finding triggers a codebase-wide search for siblings of the same pattern, a preference for a structural fix that eliminates the class (a safe API, a type that makes the illegal state unrepresentable, a linter rule), and a regression test plus a detection so the class cannot silently return.

Resilience code that retries forever or waits without limit, converting a downstream slowdown into a self-inflicted, cascading denial of service — the availability failure dressed as robustness. Countermeasure: every cross-boundary call has a timeout, a bounded retry budget with jittered backoff, and a circuit breaker; load and fault tests confirm the system fails fast and degrades rather than piling up and falling over.

Defensive logging that captures credentials, tokens, or PII in plaintext, or an audit trail an in-blast-radius compromise can rewrite to erase its tracks. Countermeasure: redact secrets and sensitive data at the logging boundary (collector-level scrubbing), never place credentials in logs by construction, and keep integrity/audit logs append-only on a path isolated from the components they record.

Error and cleanup paths that, on an unexpected condition, grant access, skip the check, or continue on corrupted state — the exception handler that returns "allow" because the deny path threw. Countermeasure: fail closed everywhere — an error in an authorization or validation path denies; a detected corruption aborts; the default in every ambiguous branch is the safe one, and the audit specifically exercises error and cleanup branches, where these defects concentrate.
